items.title: Did the Redistricting Wars Backfire on Republicans? In a Word, No.
items.author: Nate Cohn and Eve Washington
items.content: <article>The G.O.P. was able to avoid more House midterm losses — on top of the advantage it already had from gerrymandering.</article>
items.lbText:
When Republicans started redrawing congressional maps in the summer of 2025, they hoped to gain enough seats to give the party a chance to hold the House in this year’s midterm elections.

That gambit did not come close to working. The Democrats won so overwhelmingly that they easily overcame the G.O.P.’s newly drawn lines. In many cases, Democrats wound up winning the seats that the Republicans targeted. Sometimes, Democrats even gained seats in the very states where Republicans redrew the maps to their advantage.

But do Democratic gains mean the Republican effort backfired? Did Republicans lose more seats in 2026 than they would have had they left the maps alone?

Our preliminary estimate is no, the Republican effort didn’t backfire. In fact, Republicans still gained anywhere from four to seven seats as a result of the new maps, even if they didn’t pay off as Republicans hoped.

There is one state where the Republican effort seems to have backfired, if only barely: North Carolina. Elsewhere, Republicans came out ahead or the new maps didn’t make a difference either way.

items.title: Even High-Flying Democrats Found Themselves Grounded in the Mile High City
items.author: Reid J. Epstein and Lisa Lerer
items.content: <article>After a nationwide ground stop, several governors and the former secretary of transportation were among those stranded in a Denver hotel bar.</article>
items.lbText:
Pete Buttigieg could not believe what he had just watched. The former transportation secretary stood at the corner of the hotel bar in Denver, where CNN had just finished broadcasting the Trump administration’s news conference about the ground stop that stopped flights nationwide on Friday.

Mr. Buttigieg was among the thousands of Democrats who had gathered in Denver this week for a conference designed to chart the party’s future and celebrate their midterm wins. The ground stop stranded some of the party’s top rising stars and their staffs.

People accustomed to having inside information suddenly had very little.

At a table to Mr. Buttigieg’s left sat Gov. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan. They munched on Parmesan fries and checked their phones as they waited for news of their flights.

To his right, Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia scanned his Senate group chats to check for updates from secure channels and Senator Mark Warner of Virginia.

But Mr. Buttigieg, glancing up at the television, struggled to comprehend the performance of his successor, Secretary Sean Duffy.

“You can just write down the comic book asterisk swearing characters,” Mr. Buttigieg said when a New York Times reporter asked for his impressions of the news conference. “I have questions.”

The downtown hotel bar resembled the famous bar scene in “Star Wars.” The stranded politicians bemoaned the lack of information from the federal government and their inability to get home.

One New England-based operative booked a rental car and planned to drive back to Boston. Others looked up how many hours it would take to get to the East Coast on Amtrak. (The answer: more than 40.) Aides to one prominent Democratic governor, who had flown to Denver on a private jet, fielded questions from others in the bar about whether they could hitch a ride home.

A few people working for Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois — who did not come to Denver — commandeered a long table where Anne Caprara, his chief of staff, worked two phones as she juggled rumors, emergencies back home and calls from the boss. She said Mr. Pritzker was furious about the lack of information coming from the Trump administration.

“Welcome to Denver’s hottest bar, the Mos Eisley Cantina of politics,” Ms. Caprara said, referring to the “Star Wars” bar. “With ‘Veep’ characters and a ‘Terminator 2’ vibe.”

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Lisa Lerer is a national political reporter for The Times, based in New York. She has covered American politics for nearly two decades.

items.title: Trump to Meet With Putin and Xi in China, With Nuclear Proliferation on the Agenda
items.author: Katie Rogers
items.content: <article>The president plans to also discuss the war against Iran, but is not expected to bring up Russia’s war in Ukraine or the scandal that has engulfed Jensen Huang.</article>
items.lbText:
President Trump will have a joint meeting with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia during a summit in China next week, a White House spokeswoman said on Friday.

It will be the first trilateral meeting the three leaders have held together, and the third meeting Mr. Trump has had with Mr. Xi in person this year. At the meeting with Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump plans to discuss the war against Iran, but is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.

Olivia Wales, the White House spokeswoman, said that Mr. Trump would also address the threat of nuclear proliferation . U.S. officials have expressed concerns about a steady buildup of China’s arsenal in recent years, and a U.S. nuclear arms control treaty with Russia expired in February.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Ms. Wales said in a telephone briefing with reporters.

Two senior administration officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the president’s travel plans, said that Mr. Trump would travel to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila early next week. The officials said he would then travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, where he will meet with Mr. Xi and then both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin.

The officials said that Mr. Trump would be joined by the billionaire Elon Musk in Shenzhen, but added that Mr. Musk would not be part of the trilateral meeting.

Mr. Trump is prepared to discuss the “difficult” topic of Beijing’s nuclear arsenal with Mr. Xi, one of the officials said.

China maintains secretive nuclear facilities and is on track to have 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030, producing the weapons at a pace that has worried U.S. officials and analysts. On the call, the administration officials said that they did not expect any agreements on nuclear proliferation, and characterized the talks as a starting point.

Mr. Trump said this week that he had no plans to discuss with Mr. Xi the scandal that had engulfed Jensen Huang, who until this week was the chief executive of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world. Mr. Huang stepped down from his role in the wake of revelations that he had engaged in extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang , a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe is an asset of Beijing.

The officials said that the matter involving Ms. Huang was a national security issue, and did not expect Mr. Trump to discuss it with Mr. Xi during a diplomatic meeting.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

items.title: Trump Administration Delays Enforcement of Medicaid Work Requirement
items.author: Sarah Kliff and Margot Sanger-Katz
items.content: <article>The federal government had planned to require poor adults to prove they were working or lose insurance coverage starting Jan. 1. Now, it will let states wait until July.</article>
items.lbText:
The Trump administration will allow states to delay enforcement of new rules requiring low-income adults to work in order to receive Medicaid coverage, according to a letter it sent on Friday to state Medicaid directors.

The announcement, which followed a recent loss in court over a key element of the work requirement, represents a major setback for a long-sought Republican reform. It comes less than two months before the work requirements were set to begin, on Jan. 1. States can now wait until July before ending coverage for people who do not meet the work requirement, the letter said.

In the letter, Dan Brillman, who oversees Medicaid at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, acknowledged the significant burden states faced in building out new, expensive software systems to track the employment of enrollees. Hospitals have prepared massive education campaigns to help patients navigate the additional paperwork.

“We have heard directly from states about their implementation timelines, impediments to successful launches at scale,” Mr. Brillman wrote in the letter.

He added that the federal government still expected states in January to begin checking whether Medicaid enrollees are working. But for six months, they will not be required to cancel coverage for people who fail to comply, Mr. Brillman said.

The work requirement was enacted in the summer of 2025 as part of Republicans’ major tax and domestic policy legislation. It requires Medicaid enrollees without disabilities or young children to prove they worked, volunteered or attended school at least 80 hours a month in order to qualify for the program or continue enrollment in it.

items.title: House Democrats Open Inquiry After Incoming Lawmaker Accused of Sexual Harassment
items.author: Emily Davies
items.content: <article>The House Democratic campaign arm is looking into an allegation against Representative-elect Brian Poindexter of Ohio. His campaign says he “gave what he thought was an innocuous compliment to a volunteer.”</article>
items.lbText:
House Democrats are investigating Brian Poindexter, a Democrat elected last week to represent a congressional district in northeastern Ohio, after he faced an accusation of sexual harassment.

In a statement on Friday, Julie Merz, the executive director of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said the organization had “hired an independent, third-party firm to investigate any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts.”

Ms. Merz said the committee, which is the House Democratic campaign arm, would have more to say after the investigation was completed.

The investigation follows an allegation that surfaced late in the race from a woman Mr. Poindexter’s campaign described as a “volunteer.” An advocacy organization for victims of sexual misconduct described the woman as a “low-level campaign staffer.” Neither the organization nor the D.C.C.C. has specified the nature of the allegation, and the woman has not been identified.

Mr. Poindexter defeated Representative Max Miller, a Republican whose ex-wife accused him of physically abusing her and their young daughter. Mr. Miller denied the accusations, which were a focal point in the campaign.

Asked about the allegation against Mr. Poindexter, his campaign said he “gave what he thought was an innocuous compliment to a volunteer.”

items.title: Nvidia Scandal Prompts Questions of What It Means to Be a Spy
items.author: Julian E. Barnes, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan
items.content: <article>U.S. intelligence agencies believe a woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang was a Chinese asset. But there is much more that they are still assessing about her role.</article>
items.lbText:
Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, was believed to be using her affair with Nvidia’s founder to help China get around U.S. efforts to restrict access to advanced A.I. chips, people who have read U.S. intelligence reporting said.

But there remains much that intelligence agencies are still assessing about Ms. Huang including when she began working with China’s top spy agency, whether her cooperation was willing or coerced, how much direction Beijing gave her, and how much she relayed to officials there, the people said.

Her relationship with Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday, gave her potential access to crucial information about the company’s technology, Mr. Huang’s strategic thinking and his knowledge of Washington’s debates about A.I. policy.

She also had a business interest in ensuring a flow of chips to her own company, one of a number in Southeast Asia that provided Chinese tech firms with the computing power needed to train advanced artificial intelligence models.

The aftershocks of the scandal continue to play out as President Trump prepares for a trip next week to Asia, where he is scheduled to meet with President Xi Jinping of China, who has made a top priority of catching the United States in the race for A.I. dominance.

The unknowns surrounding Ms. Huang have generated intense scrutiny of how Chinese intelligence operates, prompted questions of what it means to be a spy and given backers of Mr. Huang an opening to raise questions about the extent and nature of her role.

items.title: The Numbers Behind Scott Colom’s Stunning Upset in the Mississippi Senate Race
items.author: Luke Vrotsos and Evan Reynolds
items.content: <article>To win a Senate seat in a highly polarized, deeply Republican state, Scott Colom needed a perfect storm. He got it.</article>
items.lbText:
To pull off Mississippi’s first Democratic Senate victory in more than four decades — in a state Donald J. Trump won by nearly 23 percentage points just two years ago — Scott Colom couldn’t simply ride a shifting national mood over the finish line.

A win would require high turnout among Black voters, who make up nearly 40 percent of the state’s population, and inroads with white voters. It also would not hurt if his opponent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, did worse than other Republicans on the ballot, as she had in the past.

In the end, he achieved all of that and more. Mr. Colom is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi since John C. Stennis, a staunch segregationist who opposed civil rights for much of his tenure. He will also be the first Black man to hold the position since the Reconstruction era. In a year of upheaval for the Senate, Mr. Colom’s win stood above the rest as Mississippi was the reddest seat flipped by a Democrat.

As in other Southern states this year, Black turnout in Mississippi was high. Voters in numerous majority-Black counties turned out at rates nearly as high as the 2024 presidential election — a remarkable achievement in a midterm. In some majority-Black neighborhoods, more voters turned out for this election than did so in 2024, even though that election featured the first Black woman presidential nominee.

The Black share of the Mississippi electorate rose to 33 percent in 2026, compared with 30 percent two years ago, according to Times Voter Trends , which estimates how demographic groups voted using a variety of data sources. Black voters in the state are overwhelmingly Democratic, and 91 percent of them supported Mr. Colom. An increase of a few percentage points in the Black share of the electorate translates to large gains for the party.

items.title: Trump Officials Press Congress to Renew Spying Law in Lame-Duck Session
items.author: Charlie Savage and Dustin Volz
items.content: <article>The request to extend a high-profile warrantless surveillance law would add a thorny issue during waning Republican control.</article>
items.lbText:
The Trump administration pressed top lawmakers on Friday to extend a high-profile warrantless surveillance law within the next month, moving to resolve a thorny policy dispute in the last weeks of a Republican-controlled Congress.

In a letter to congressional leaders, three top national security officials in the administration — Todd Blanche, the attorney general, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, and John Ratcliffe, the C.I.A. director — said President Trump had urged them to extend the law known as Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act now.

“As you know, Section 702 is the single most indispensable tool we have to keep our homeland and the American people safe,” they wrote. “It enables our intelligence community to detect and disrupt terrorist plots, cyber intrusions, and weapons proliferation. No other authority can replace it.”

But any push to bring a Section 702 bill to the floor — either by itself, or bundled with some larger package like the annual National Defense Authorization Act — appeared likely to set off a new round of heated contention. Privacy and civil liberties advocates in both parties have been pushing to add new limits, like requiring the government to obtain permission from a judge before deliberately gaining access to the messages of Americans swept up under the program.

In a statement, Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat and proponent of adding more limits to the program, said the issue should wait for the next Congress, when Democrats will have control.

items.title: 5 Takeaways from Joe Biden’s Memoir: The Debate, Dropping Out and Advice From Romney
items.author: Tim Balk
items.content: <article>The 46th president defends his decision to run for re-election, which many in his party now regard as a mistake, and revisits the disastrous debate that forced him to end his campaign.</article>
items.lbText:
Former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., at times defiant and defensive, describes his fateful decision to run for re-election in 2024, his immediate reaction to the debate that derailed his campaign and his exasperation with Prime Minister of Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in a new memoir, “Promise Me, America.”

Here are five takeaways from the 480-page book, scheduled to be released on Tuesday, at what would have been the rough midpoint of Mr. Biden’s second term. The 83-year-old former president, who has aggressive prostate cancer, has scaled back promotion of the memoir because of his condition.

Mr. Biden writes that he solidified his decision to run for re-election after discussing the idea with top advisers at the White House in 2023.

The reception, he recalls, was supportive and unanimous. At the time of the meeting, Mr. Biden writes, the campaign was already starting to kick into gear: He had TV ads and an announcement prepared.

“We went around the room,” writes Mr. Biden, who was just past his 80th birthday, had a drooping approval rating and had once portrayed his presidency as a bridge to the next generation of Democrats. “Everyone offered their thoughts on the race. Everyone was in. There was no demurral or dissent. I was in.”

In her own memoir published last year , “107 Days,” former Vice President Kamala Harris said Mr. Biden’s decision to run again was “recklessness” and that she should “perhaps” have advised him against it. But Ms. Harris wrote that she was in “the worst position to make the case.”

items.title: Democrats Vie for Support in Race for Top Senate Job
items.author: Carl Hulse
items.content: <article>Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said he wouldn’t run for president to focus on his leadership challenge to Senator Chuck Schumer, who remained confident he would prevail.</article>
items.lbText:
The Democratic battle for Senate majority leader intensified on Friday as Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland put aside his presidential ambitions to push forward in his campaign to challenge Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the current leader, and lined up supporters.

Appearing at a Democratic event in Denver on the future of the party, Mr. Van Hollen, who announced his challenge on Thursday night, said that he had ruled out a presidential run in 2028 after the sweeping Democratic wins on Nov. 3. Some Democrats had suggested that Mr. Van Hollen was jumping into the majority leader contest to raise his visibility and court progressive voters ahead of 2028, but he said that was not the case.

“I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people,” Mr. Van Hollen said in disclosing that he was no longer pursuing a White House bid. “I think this is a really important moment for our country, and that we can’t go back to business as usual in the United States Senate.”

He also gained some public backing from senators who will decide the contest, even as he acknowledged he was the “underdog” in the race against Mr. Schumer, who was a key architect and funder of the successful Democratic effort to retake the Senate and has led Democrats there since 2016.

Senator Jeff Merkley, the Oregon Democrat in line to be chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee, said he was supporting Mr. Van Hollen, posting on social media that he had seen him “rally support for the people against the powerful time and time again.”

Also endorsing Mr. Van Hollen on social media was Peggy Flanagan, the senator-elect from Minnesota, who wrote that Mr. Van Hollen “is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change.” She was among the newly elected members who had campaigned on calls for a leadership change.

items.title: Russia Revives Demand That NATO Retrench to Secure Ukraine Deal
items.author: Anton Troianovski, Andrew E. Kramer, Jeanna Smialek, David E. Sanger and Eric Schmitt
items.content: <article>The hard-line position of Russian officials in closed-door negotiations about ending the war thrusts European security into the heart of the talks.</article>
items.lbText:
Two months before Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, it issued a series of far-reaching demands , including that NATO pull its troops back to positions they held in 1997, before the Western alliance expanded toward Russia’s borders.

Now, in closed-door negotiations with President Trump’s envoys this week about how to end the war in Ukraine, the Russians have revived that stance — in some cases word for word — in an effort to attain a larger victory after five years and hundreds of thousands of deaths.

Moscow’s unyielding position was laid out in a paper that Russian officials circulated this week, according to a copy obtained by The New York Times from a person involved in the talks.

The paper, whose authenticity was confirmed by another person with knowledge of the negotiations, shows that President Vladimir V. Putin has scarcely budged on his core objectives after more than 20 months of diplomacy by the Trump administration to end the conflict.

Russia’s demands that NATO pull back forces from its eastern flank in Poland and the Baltics thrust the question of European security into the heart of the negotiations over Ukraine. And they detail the objective behind Mr. Putin’s public statements. The Russian leader has continually insisted that what he calls the “root causes” of the war — Russia’s wide-ranging grievances with both NATO and Ukraine — be addressed before he stops fighting.

The document also underscores how the economic inducements that Mr. Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have offered Mr. Putin have yet to secure concessions from Moscow. To critics, the United States risks enabling Mr. Putin’s long-running attempt to reassert a Soviet-era sphere of influence as far away as Central Asia.

items.title: Hakeem Jeffries Pushes to Lock Down House Speakership, With No Challenger Emerging
items.author: Annie Karni
items.content: <article>Facing resistance from the left but no challenger, the Democratic leader is sewing up support from key coalitions as his allies say he deserves a unanimous vote.</article>
items.lbText:
Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, is pressing to wrap up his nomination to be speaker next week quickly and overwhelmingly, leaving potential detractors little room to maneuver around him even as some of them complain about an undemocratic process.

His allies this week began asking Democrats to sign a letter publicly signaling their backing for Mr. Jeffries ahead of the House Democrats’ closed-door leadership elections on Wednesday. Some of them think he deserves to be elected unanimously during that session, bypassing a vote by secret ballot that would give any dissenters a chance to register opposition. It would be a show of overwhelming unity and support, although Mr. Jeffries has not yet indicated whether he is seeking it.

But his allies are soliciting group endorsements to lock in backing from large factions, effectively shutting down any conversation about other options in an implicit sign that his nomination is inevitable. The New Democrat Coalition, a group of 114 center-left House Democrats and at least 40 members-elect, issued one such statement in support of Mr. Jeffries this week.

Mr. Jeffries has been meeting privately both with incumbents and new members to make his case, although he has yet to reach out to every newly elected member of the House. He is set next week to attend the Congressional Progressive Caucus board meeting, according to two people familiar with the plans, and his goal is to be in direct contact with every member by Wednesday.

The quiet campaign comes as Mr. Jeffries, in line to be the first Black speaker after presiding over sweeping Democratic victories and winning a historic majority, is facing some resistance from an energized left clamoring for a new face at the helm of the party for the new Congress. No one has stepped forward to challenge him.

items.title: African Miss Universe Contestants Struggle to Get U.S. Visas
items.author: Matthew Mpoke Bigg
items.content: <article>A crackdown on entry by some citizens of African countries by the U.S. immigration officials means that some contestants might not get visas in time to attend the pageant in Puerto Rico this month.</article>
items.lbText:
At least two African contestants for Miss Universe said they were in danger of missing the pageant in Puerto Rico this month because they had not secured U.S. visas amid a crackdown by the Trump administration.

One contestant, Miss Zambia, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka, said she would not travel to the annual event on Nov. 24 because she had not received her visa, according to Arm Model Management, which said it was the franchise holder of Miss Zambia 2026.

Her nonattendance is “linked to the United States presidential travel restrictions affecting Zambia and other African nations,” the agency said in a statement on social media. “She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves.”

The contestant from Zimbabwe, Roseanna Hall, said on social media that she, too, had not received a U.S. visa. “I will not give up,” she said. Contestants from South Sudan and the Republic of Congo also faced delays, according to news reports.

The Miss Universe organization did not immediately reply to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security also did not respond to a similar request. It was unclear why the contestants had not received visas.

The social media page of the Miss Universe organization listed 20 African countries among its contestants for the pageant to held in the U.S. territory.

The Trump administration has curtailed several avenues to legal migration to the United States as part of a crackdown, including visa bans and restrictions that have hit African countries hard. The administration in January imposed full or partial travel bans and visa restrictions on 36 countries, and 29 of those are in Africa.

In December, the Trump administration widened travel restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while keeping in place full restrictions for citizens of the Republic of Congo and adding them for South Sudan.

Homeland Security has said it was “slamming the door shut on the foreign invaders who have undermined our national security.”

Citizens of African countries have for decades complained of draconian visa rules imposed by the governments of the United States and European countries. Governments say the restrictions aim to control migration and prevent fraud, but many Africans say they impede legitimate professional, business and study opportunities and stop family members from attending occasions such as births, weddings and funerals.

Those restrictions have become more severe since public attitudes in many Western countries have turned against immigration over the past decade.

Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

items.title: Supreme Court Set to Hear Trump’s Ban on Asylum Claims at Border
items.author: Ann E. Marimow and Hamed Aleaziz
items.content: <article>Lower courts have ruled against the policy, which has effectively shut down avenues for people seeking asylum protections and to remain in the United States.</article>
items.lbText:
The Supreme Court announced on Friday that it will review the legality of the Trump administration’s policy of categorically denying asylum claims from people crossing the southern border, taking up another major test of the president’s immigration agenda.

On President Trump’s first day back in office, he effectively shut down the ability of people fearing torture and persecution to apply for asylum protections at the border and then remain in the United States, declaring there was an “invasion” along the southern border. In a proclamation, he invoked what he called “the inherent right and duty of the executive branch to defend our national sovereignty.”

Immigration rights group quickly challenged the proclamation, and lower courts have found it to be illegal. But it has still largely been in force under a temporary court order. The Supreme Court case is expected to be the culmination of years of litigation over the ability of the government to prohibit migrants from claiming asylum at the border.

This Supreme Court term, which began in October and will conclude next summer, is shaping up to be dominated by Mr. Trump’s aggressive immigration policies. In December, the court will review the administration’s efforts to deport immigrants to so-called third countries where they have no ties, including nations that have faced allegations of human rights abuses. Next year, the court will consider the administration’s policy of indefinitely detaining immigrants who crossed the border illegally years ago.

In the asylum case the justices accepted on Friday, a central question is whether the president can override immigration law set by Congress. During the first Trump administration, officials struggled to come up with restrictive asylum policies at the border that would survive judicial scrutiny.

In his second term, the president adopted the prohibition on asylum claims at the border and has been fighting over the policy in court. D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, told the justices in court filings that their intervention was “urgently warranted” in part because the policy was Mr. Trump’s “main tool for stemming an unprecedented crisis of uncontrolled illegal entry.”

items.title: Trump Signals New Strategy on Iran: A Waiting Game
items.author: David E. Sanger
items.content: <article>The administration appears to be moving toward a long-term economic pressure campaign as President Trump expresses little urgency in securing a nuclear agreement.</article>
items.lbText:
President Trump says he is leaning toward a new solution to the Iran nuclear crisis: Declare it is over, even if not much has changed.

Mr. Trump and his team have taken to asserting that they have the Iranians right where they want them. They say they no longer need a new nuclear agreement that would remove potential bomb fuel from the country, or to limit Iran’s missile capability, two of the leading reasons the president cited 10 months ago for going to war.

Mr. Trump appears — at least for now — to have rejected a series of military options that would involve intense, if time-limited, attacks on military installations, nuclear sites and even some energy infrastructure.

All the talk this year of sending in commandos to seize roughly 970 pounds of uranium from the country, enriched to a near-bomb-grade level of 60 percent purity, has been abandoned, albeit for the moment. So has the detailed analysis of whether America’s biggest bunker busters are powerful enough to get deep into Pickaxe Mountain, a site U.S. intelligence believes — but is not sure — is the location of advanced centrifuges that can purify uranium into bomb fuel.

In comments to reporters this week in Paris, where he was attending a meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 7, Secretary of State Marco Rubio described an approach best characterized as strategic patience: waiting for sanctions on Iran to take their toll and ultimately crack their government.

“At this point, the economic campaign and the pressure and the devastation that our economic campaign is having on the Iranian regime is working so well that the president really doesn’t have any need to conduct major combat operations,” Mr. Rubio said.

items.title: Bessent Faults Commerce Dept. for Failing to Blacklist Megaspeed
items.author: Ana Swanson
items.content: <article>The Treasury secretary blamed the department for not sanctioning the Singaporean firm and said that Nvidia employees should be held accountable if they sidestepped the law.</article>
items.lbText:
Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, blamed the Commerce Department on Friday for the government’s failure to sanction the Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed, saying that other departments had pushed for the measure but that Commerce “has the pen.”

The Treasury, Defense and State Departments and the U.S. trade representative were all in favor of putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist called the entity list for months, but the Commerce Department is in charge of that authority, Mr. Bessent said on CNBC on Friday.

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said, adding, “Treasury and my deputy has been pushing for this for months at the deputies level.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” he said. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

Frustration is boiling over within the administration and on Capitol Hill about Megaspeed, the company led by a woman U.S. intelligence deemed to be an asset for the Chinese government.

The woman, Alice Huang, had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang. Mr. Huang resigned from his company on Thursday in the wake of revelations about that and another affair, sending the company’s stock price cratering.
